entry.evidence: the results from different types of rock may be contradictory and not comparable, which makes comprehensive conclusions impossible

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML full text and PDF)

steps.action: Posed the problem that weathering indices from different lithologies are not comparable, so regional reconstructions of hiatal surfaces fail.
steps.quote: the results from different types of rock may be contradictory and not comparable, which makes comprehensive conclusions impossible

steps.action: Built a fracture classification (tectonic, pre/syn-weathering filled, late void, burial-overprinted) and an ImageJ thin-section protocol for measuring fracture area, with its statistical error stated.
steps.quote: The statistical error is less than 250 µm2 with a mean value of approximately 55 µm2.

steps.action: Compiled published UCS and CIA data for basaltic and granitic rocks and fitted two rock-specific exponential UCS-CIA regressions (Eqs. 1-2, Fig. 4).
steps.quote: this study compiled data and created a regression out of two rock-specific empirical relationships between UCS and the chemical index of alteration (CIA)

steps.action: Defined the index of physical weathering (IPW, Eq. 3) and its strength-normalized form IPWN for two tectonic-fracture situations (Eqs. 4-6).
steps.quote: one method is to normalize the IPW with the corresponding susceptibility to physical weathering for each type of rock

steps.action: Tested 3x3, 3x5 and 4x5 view grids per thin section and chose 15 views because the mean IPW stabilizes (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: The results indicate that the variation in the average value of the IPW approaches stable values after 15 visions independent of rock type.

steps.action: Defined total weathering mass (TWM, integral of the White and Brantley 2003 time-dependent rate law) and chemical weathering ability (CWA), and a CIA normalization to a reference rock via λ, n, λN and CIAN (Eqs. 7-13).
steps.quote: an appropriate solution is to first set a reference rock, and evaluate the chemical index of alteration of the reference rock

steps.action: Selected three drill cores through the post-Variscan nonconformity with different basement lithologies and at least 13 m depth to exclude modern weathering.
steps.quote: penetration through the Variscan nonconformity at a depth of at least 13 m to rule out modern weathering

steps.action: Collected 52 samples from paleosol to fresh rock and characterized them by polarizing microscopy, SEM, XRD, XRF/ICP-MS, C-O isotopes and fracture-angle measurement.
steps.quote: In total, 52 samples were collected around the nonconformity.

steps.action: Excluded a tectonic origin of the fractures because the rose diagrams of fracture angles show no preferential direction (Fig. 12).
steps.quote: Fractures along the entire drill cores indicate a random distribution of angles. A preferential angle distribution does not exist.

steps.action: Computed IPW profiles from fracture-area ratios (average of 15 views per thin section) for each fracture type and core (Fig. 13).
steps.quote: The fracture area ratio (IPW) values are represented by the average of 15 values from each thin section.

steps.action: Used fresh parent-rock thin sections as a reference showing no fractures, so no parent-rock (tectonic) fracture area had to be subtracted.
steps.quote: However, thin sections from the fresh rocks at all drillings do not show fractures.

steps.action: Computed the fluid δ18O implied by the measured calcite under a surface-weathering scenario (25 °C) and a burial scenario (290 °C) using the Friedman and O'Neil fractionation (Eqs. 14-15, Fig. 14).
steps.quote: If all the calcite within the weathering profile of GA1 and GA2 was formed during surface weathering under the temperature of 25 ℃

steps.action: Rejected a weathering origin of the fracture carbonate in favour of burial diagenesis and reclassified carbonate-filled fractures as originally void.
steps.quote: the calcite within GA1 and GA2 should all have formed during burial diagenesis rather than chemical weathering

steps.action: Computed IPWN profiles for granodiorite, basaltic andesite and granite using UCS from the CIA-UCS regressions (Fig. 15).
steps.quote: The IPWN values of the granodiorite in the GA2 drill core increase from 0.22 at the bottom to 3.85 at the top.

steps.action: For the gabbro-like 2.6 m sample in GA2, replaced the granitic UCS-CIA relation with a published UCS for slightly weathered gabbro (43.1 MPa).
steps.quote: Here, the arithmetic average value of 43.1 was applied.

steps.action: Reported bulk major-element and CIA profiles along the three cores (Fig. 16).
steps.quote: The results of bulk major element concentrations are listed in Supplementary B (Table S1)

steps.action: Took from the authors' earlier study that the profiles were overprinted by K-metasomatism.
steps.quote: The results acquired by Liang et al (52) indicate that the weathering profile in the area was overprinted by K-metasomatism.

steps.action: Corrected K2O with the Panahi et al. (2000) method before computing CIA (Eqs. 16-17).
steps.quote: To correct the K content within the weathering profiles, the method proposed by Panahi et al. (75) was applied.

steps.action: Checked the K correction against the expected A-CN weathering trend in the A-CN-K diagram (Fig. 17B).
steps.quote: With the correction, the weathering trend for all the drill cores was parallel to the A-CN joint

steps.action: Varied the assumed weathering duration (0.01, 0.1 and 1 Myr) when computing TWM and CWA, because the timescale is uncertain (Fig. 18).
steps.quote: a wide range for the duration of weathering from ten thousand to one million years was applied

steps.action: Normalized CIA to the BK2/05 granite as reference lithology, giving CIAs and CIAsN profiles that follow the original trends.
steps.quote: fresh granite samples from drill core BK2/05 are set as the reference lithology

steps.action: Regressed IPW against CIA and CIAsN for each rock type and found positive correlations with rock-specific slopes, stronger after normalization (Fig. 20).
steps.quote: Although in all cases a positive correlation can be observed, the inclination of the regression line is different for each rock type.

steps.action: Inferred a trend toward more humid climate from rising chemical and falling physical weathering intensity across the sections.
steps.quote: the climate exhibits a gradual trend toward more humid conditions

steps.action: Applied the Sheldon (2006) and Stinchcomb et al. (2016) paleosol-paleoclimate models to the same geochemical data and compared their MAP and MAT trends with IPWN and CIAN (Table 2).
steps.quote: to show the robustness of the methods and results proposed in this study, the major elements employed in this case study are used

steps.action: Explained the mismatch of the Sheldon-based MAP for the granite and granodiorite by K-feldspar inflating CIA-K, rather than revising the indices.
steps.quote: An explanation is that the parent rock (granodiorite and granite) of the samples contains K-feldspar

steps.action: Kept IPWN and CIAN, with their workflow, as a new way to quantify physical and chemical weathering intensity jointly across lithologies.
steps.quote: allows for the first time the simultaneous quantification of the physical and chemical weathering intensity at subaerial paleo-surfaces in the geological record

tree.answer: Weathering degree differs by lithology under the same intensity, so indices are not comparable
No; weathering intensity is latent, inferred from fracture area, CIA and rock strength
Build normalized indices (IPWN, CIAN) and demonstrate them on drill cores
Only for auxiliaries: tectonic vs weathering fractures; weathering vs burial carbonate
Yes for auxiliaries: preferential vs random fracture angles; meteoric vs hydrothermal fluid δ18O
Found: existing drill cores through a past nonconformity
Partly: view-grid and duration variations, two independent paleoclimate models; granite mismatch explained away
Indices kept as a demonstrated capability
Not documented; no review file supplied

end.claim: The normalized indices IPWN and CIAN and their workflow allow physical and chemical weathering intensity at paleo-surfaces to be quantified together and compared across rock types.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the definition of the strength-normalized IPWN and the CWA-based CIA normalization to a reference rock, there would be no rock-independent weathering-intensity indices to claim.

gates.evidence: The drill cores were chosen to demonstrate the method (different lithologies, more than 13 m depth; §3.1 ¶3), not under a stated hypothesis. The method's output could have disagreed with two independent paleoclimate models (§4.2 ¶5-6), and partly did for the granite MAP, which was explained by K-feldspar rather than counted as a failure. The grid size, duration range and reference rock were set or chosen alongside the data; nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: ImageJ software for manual polygon outlining and area measurement of fractures
Uniaxial compressive and tensile strength as susceptibility to fracturing (UTS about 0.1 UCS)
MultiPrep-GV Isoprime II isotope-ratio mass spectrometer with NBS-19 calibration
PANalytical X'Pert diffractometer with RIR quantification from ICDD PDF-2/PDF-4 (MacDiff)
Partial least squares regression and nonlinear spline in the Stinchcomb et al. paleoclimate model

novelty_claims.quote: allows for the first time the simultaneous quantification of the physical and chemical weathering intensity at subaerial paleo-surfaces in the geological record
However, an index for physical weathering is still not available.
This study suggested a new index of physical weathering (IPW) to quantify physical weathering in paleoweathering profiles at the microscale.
To date, this has been not linked to specific rock types as addressed in this paper.
This offers a completely new spectrum of possibilities to quantitatively compare weathering and climatic conditions at the regional scale

limits:
Composition is none_fits: the walk runs problem, then a new method, then a demonstration case study. It is not capability_first (the question comes first) and has no rival claims at the level of the headline claim; rivals appear only for auxiliaries (fracture origin, carbonate origin).

The capability is characterized only partly. A statistical error for fracture-area outlining and a view-number stability test are reported, but there is no uncertainty propagated to IPWN or CIAN, no inter-operator test of the manual outlining, and no test of CWA as a measure of susceptibility against independent weathering data.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Climate trend toward more humid conditions (§4.2 ¶1): best_explanation at most, and weakly supported.
- Rock-dependent IPW-CIA relationships (§4.1 ¶6): regularity_in_range on very few samples per rock type.
- Burial origin of fracture carbonate (§3.3.3 ¶6): best_explanation.

IPWN could not be computed for the gabbroic diorite (no UCS-CIA relation; §4.1 ¶4). The opposite IPWN trend in the granite is attributed to heterogeneity without a test (§4.1 ¶2). The granite MAP mismatch is explained post hoc (§4.2 ¶6).

The text has internal inconsistencies:
- Eq. 6 is labelled PWIN.
- "Applying Eq. (6)" for the pyroxene rates likely means Eq. (7) (inference).
- Depths are inconsistent, e.g. the basaltic andesite "topmost part (13.9 m)" and the BK2/05 "fresh part (10.8 m)" against a weathering depth of about 2 m.
- The ordering of sections used for the climate trend is not explained.

No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgements mention two anonymous reviewers, but changes made in review cannot be reconstructed. The reason for the 10x10 magnification choice ("best results") and the order in which the analyses were actually done are not documented.

disagreements.target: Traditional chemical weathering indices (CIA, PIA, CIW, Σ bases/Al) used across lithologies
disagreements.support: The paper argues from mineral-composition and susceptibility differences that raw index values are not comparable across rock types, and proposes CWA-based normalization.
disagreements.quote: even under the same weathering intensity, the weathering degree for different types of rock is different

disagreements.target: Rock Weathering Classification diagram (Aggisttalis et al. 1996) and derived engineering classifications
disagreements.support: The paper notes these are qualitative and mix physical and chemical features, and offers a quantitative fracture-area index instead.
disagreements.quote: However, a physical index specifically for modern and paleoweathering profiles has yet to be created.

disagreements.target: Regional-scale physical weathering methods (Shoenfelt et al. 2019; Qin et al. 2006)
disagreements.support: These methods are stated to be suitable only at regional scale, not for local profiles; no new evidence is offered.
disagreements.quote: However, these methods are only suitable for investigations on a regional scale

disagreements.target: Previous paleoweathering studies emphasizing absolute chemical weathering degree
disagreements.support: The paper adds petrographic fracture analysis and rock-type normalization to address the neglect of physical weathering.
disagreements.quote: The characteristics formed by physical weathering are less considered.

disagreements.target: Harnois (1988) and Maynard (1992) removal of K2O from the CIA
disagreements.support: Removing K ignores the associated Al, so the method suits plagioclase but not K-feldspar- or biotite-bearing rocks; the Panahi correction is used instead.
disagreements.quote: However, it is not appropriate to evaluate the weathering degree of the parent lithologies that contain K-feldspar and/or biotite

disagreements.support: The model ignores burial-diagenetic overprint, so Ca and K are corrected before it is applied.
disagreements.quote: However, the model does not consider the overprint of burial diagenesis.

disagreements.target: Sheldon (2006) CIA-K precipitation estimate applied to K-feldspar-bearing parent rocks
disagreements.support: For granite and granodiorite the CIA-K-based MAP is too high relative to the petrographically moderate weathering, which is attributed to K-feldspar.
disagreements.quote: [...] a higher value of CIA-K compared to its actual chemical index of alteration

alternatives_considered.reason: Orientations are difficult to measure in drill cores

alternatives_considered.chosen: Burial-diagenetic origin of fracture carbonate (treated as void fractures)
alternatives_considered.reason: Implied fluid δ18O at 25 °C versus 290 °C, plus coexisting dolomite and quartz

alternatives_considered.chosen: Published UCS for slightly weathered gabbro (43.1) for the 2.6 m GA2 sample

alternatives_considered.reason: Granite CWA is moderate, so CIAsN does not exceed 100

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both Sheldon (2006) and Stinchcomb et al. (2016) paleoclimate models
alternatives_considered.reason: To extend applications and show robustness
